v20_abstract: Autonomous LLM agents now routinely manipulate file systems and APIs in high-stakes software engineering workflows. While reactive frameworks like AgentSpec monitor individual actions, they fail to account for unsafe outcomes that emerge only from a cumulative sequence of individually compliant steps. This survey analyzes LLM safety across four methodological areas, identifying a fundamental disconnect between a single action enforcement and the reality of multi- stage exploits. We find that the field lacks not only proactive, sequence- level mechanisms for code agents but also the formal probabilistic models required to bound stochastic behavior and behavioral drift. Moreover, current benchmarks are shown to be predominantly static, failing to capture the complexity of real-world trajectories. By mapping these systemic gaps, we define the requirements for a proactive safety roadmap, emphasizing the transition toward dynamic, sequence-aware enforcement and multi-step evaluation metrics to secure agents in production environments.

title: Large Action Models: A Unified Smart Framework for Autonomous Intelligent Systems
publication: 2026 International Conference on Smart Futuristic Technology Icsft 2026
recovered_title: Large Action Models: A Unified Smart Framework for Autonomous Intelligent Systems
v20_recovered_title: Large Action Models: A Unified Smart Framework for Autonomous Intelligent Systems
v20_abstract: Large Action Models (LAMs) represent the next generation of smart autonomous frameworks, transitioning artificial intelligence from passive content generation to goal-directed action execution in digital and physical environments. This systematic survey provides the first unified taxonomy and architectural framework for LAM-based intelligent systems through rigorous analysis of 50 peer-reviewed papers spanning 2023-2025. We introduce a novel five-dimensional classification framework encompassing action space, planning mechanisms, learning paradigms, deployment contexts, and safety architectures. Our comparative analysis reveals critical performance gaps: current LAMs achieve only 12-20% success rates on complex benchmarks versus 72% human performance, with action trajectory data being 100-1000× more expensive than text data. We provide the first systematic evaluation methodology for LAM surveys, synthesize architectural patterns from commercial systems (Rabbit R1, xLAM, Claude Computer Use) and research prototypes (RT-X, Agent S), and identify three fundamental bottlenecks: data efficiency, sim-to-real transfer (30-50% degradation), and safety verification. Our work establishes LAMs as a distinct paradigm in smart frameworks and intelligent technologies, bridging theory and practice while outlining actionable research directions for next-generation human-centric autonomous systems.
